opening.headline: You learn how to understand why the same prompt yields different results when the model changes, and how to distinguish what needs to be adjusted when reusing it.
body: Let's assume we migrate a prompt for classifying customer inquiries from Model A to Model B without changing a single character in the prompt. The response format, length, and tone change significantly, and the post-processing code breaks. If model switching is treated as a change to a single configuration value, such differences are only discovered after launch.

In this class, we first observe how the same prompt produces different responses across various models. Next, we learn about model-specific instruction differences, how to refine prompts based on evaluation results, techniques to reduce reimplementation costs using standard templates, and we follow a case study of the prompt refinement procedure when switching models.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: One can explain why prompt portability has limitations.
When changing a model, it is possible to identify the elements that require retraining.

screens.title: Changing the model yields different results for the same prompt.
screens.lead: First, change the model and then review the scenario where the post-processing code is corrupted.

visual.alt: A scene where the same prompt passes through two models, producing answers in different formats, causing the post-processing code to fail.
labels: Classify customer inquiries into exactly one of the following: order_status, return_policy, technical_issue, cancel_order, other.
This is an inquiry regarding the delivery status.

paragraphs: There is a service that classifies customer inquiries. The prompt instructs the model to classify the inquiry into only one of five predefined labels. Since the model returned only the label as a single word, the post-processing code was designed to read the entire response as a label.

Let's move this prompt to the B model, which appended a sentence explaining the label. The post-processing code can no longer read the response as a label and fails. The prompt sentence has not changed a single character, yet its format, length, and tone have changed.
Model changes are only discovered after release when a single setting is altered. The question for this lesson is: How far does the prompt remain unchanged, and what needs to be re-tuned?

callout.label: Note
callout.text: This scene is a hypothetical example for illustrative purposes. It is not actual output records from a real model.

screens.outro: First, let me reflect on my experience of moving a prompt.

screens.title: Have you ever tried transferring a prompt to another model?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever transferred a prompt to another model? What was the first difference you noticed after transferring it?
items.answer: The first difference that catches the eye is typically one of three: format, length, or compliance. Format can break post-processing code, length can alter cost and latency, and compliance affects accuracy. Determining which of these applies is the first step in tuning.

items.prompt: How did you verify this difference? Did you read it visually for a few instances, or did you compare it against the same input bundle?
items.answer: Reading a few examples quickly may lead to missing important details. OpenAI's accuracy optimization documentation starts with examining evaluation sets composed of evaluation questions and answers, and analyzing failure cases. To objectively observe differences, comparisons must be made using the same input batches.

If corrections are not recorded, the same trial and error will be repeated when switching to a different model next. The rationale for what and why improvements were made must be preserved so that future migrations know where to verify.

screens.outro: Now we will verify how different models respond differently to the same prompt.

screens.title: Response differences across models for the same prompt
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the virtual responses from three models for the same prompt. These responses are examples created for illustrative purposes.

tabs.label: prompt
tabs.body:
The same prompt is sent to all three models.

```text
Classify the customer inquiry into exactly one of the following: order_status, return_policy, technical_issue, cancel_order, other.

Inquiry: The shoes I ordered yesterday haven't shipped yet.
```

The instruction is clear. Yet the responses take different forms depending on the model.

tabs.label: Model A
tabs.body:
`order_status`

Only a single word label was output. The post-processing code reads the label from the entire response, so it operates without issues. This service was originally designed to match Model A's habits.

tabs.label: Model B
tabs.body:
`order_status`: This inquiry asks about shipping status, so it has been classified under the corresponding label.

A reason sentence has been appended alongside the label. The content is correct, but the post-processing code fails because it does not match any of the entries when comparing the entire response to the label.

tabs.label: Model C
tabs.body:
`cancel_order`

Instead of sending ambiguous cases from other queries to `other`, the closest label was selected. The format is correct, but due to different interpretation criteria for instructions, the classification results differ.

tabs.label: Cause of the difference
tabs.body:
The difference among the three responses comes from the model itself, not from the prompt. The way the model interprets instructions, its inherent verbosity, and its default reasoning behavior vary across models. Therefore, identical input does not guarantee identical behavior.

Thus, when switching models, one should not stop at visually reading a few responses; instead, comparisons must be made across models regarding format, length, and adherence to instructions using the same input batch.

screens.outro: Besides format differences, there are variations in how requests and responses are processed depending on the model. I will verify this next.

screens.title: Model-specific instruction differences: when the previous method gets stuck
screens.lead: Select an item to expand, and check the elements that vary by model, even outside the prompt sentence.

items.title: The default values for incidents have changed.
items.body: According to the Migration Guide for Claude Sonnet 5.5, requests without a thinking field are executed using adaptive reasoning. In Sonnet 4.6 and earlier models and Haiku 4.5, the same request was executed without any reasoning. The default behavior differs depending on the model.

items.title: Response handling codes are affected.
items.body: Responses may begin with "thinking blocks," so code that assumes the first item is text, as in content[0].text, may fail. The guide recommends reading responses by block type. Code that parses response structure is part of its portability.

items.title: Some request settings result in a 400 error.
items.body: In Sonnet 5.5, thinking budget, sampling parameters, assistant prefill, and forced tool choice cause a 400 error. The Fable 5.1 guide also alerts users to a 400 error when using assistant prefill and recommends including system prompt instructions. The approach of fixing the response beginning with prefill should be moved to output format instructions.

items.title: Same family lines can differ in inference strength.
items.body: The OpenAI model selection document explains that different tasks are suited to different models and reasoning strengths. For example, Luna's low reasoning strength is well-suited for fine-grained editing and simple data extraction, while Astra's high reasoning strength is better matched to complex analysis. Even within the same provider, changing settings can lead to different results.

items.title: Conclusion: Embodiment exists beyond the prompt.
items.body: Prompt text is not the only aspect of portability; request parameters and response handling are also part of it. When migrating to a new model, first read the changelog in the model's migration guide, and then adjust the prompt accordingly.

screens.outro: Now that the difference has been understood, we will examine a systematic reduction approach based on performance evaluation and standard templates.

screens.title: Evaluation-based realignment and standard templates
screens.lead: Compare methods of measuring and reducing the difference by transitioning between two states, and how to structure these methods into a framework.

states.label: Evaluation-based realignment
states.body:
OpenAI's accuracy optimization document begins with prompt engineering, establishes a baseline through evaluation, and then explains how to adjust based on analyzing why answers are incorrect. The evaluation consists of sets of questions and answers, and the document describes a good baseline as one that includes over 20 question-answer pairs and has analyzed failure reasons.

The adjustment axis consists of two components: **context optimization**, which enhances response accuracy by filling in information the model does not inherently know, and **LLM optimization**, which improves consistency in format, tone, and reasoning. Differences in format arising from switching models are closer to the latter.

OpenAI's model selection document also recommends comparing results with the same input and selecting the lightest setting that satisfies quality criteria.

states.label: Standard template
states.body:
The standard template divides a prompt into a fixed structure and variable components.

- **Fixed structure**: role, task, output format, example slots  
- **Model-specific overrides**: variations in instructions required only for specific models  
- **Evaluation input bundle**: representative inputs and expected outputs stored alongside the template  

This approach allows the fixed structure to remain unchanged when switching models, requiring only modifications to the override items. By preserving the evaluation input bundle, identical bundles can be directly compared with a new model. Additionally, any changed instructions are recorded in the overrides and can be referenced during subsequent migrations.

screens.outro: Now, let's proceed with an example of the procedure of adjusting the prompt when replacing a model.

screens.title: Explanation: Prompt Retuning Procedure During Model Replacement
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down the model replacement process for the inquiry classification service step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: case
steps.body: Replace the classification service from model A to model B. Instruct the prompt to classify only among one of the five labels, and the post-processing code reads the response as a label.

steps.title: Fix the baseline
steps.body: The current prompt, representative input set, and expected output are fixed as a baseline. The representative inputs include not only simple queries but also ambiguous queries and queries that cross label boundaries. A baseline must be established in order to objectively categorize subsequent differences.

steps.title: Same input is returned to classify the difference
steps.body: In the B model, the same input batch is returned for comparison against the baseline. Differences are categorized by type: attaching a sentence to a label is a format difference, violating specified rules is a compliance difference, and having a different label itself is an accuracy difference.

steps.title: Adjusts according to the type
steps.body: Format differences strengthen the output instructions in the system prompt by clearly specifying rules, such as only outputting labels without adding any other sentences. Accuracy differences enhance examples for ambiguous queries. Tuning is done one aspect at a time, with repeated review after each adjustment.

steps.title: Matches request parameters and response handling
steps.body: Changing only the prompt is not sufficient. Align the request parameters and response handling code with the changes listed in the B model's migration guide. For example, if a section previously fixed the response using prefill, move it to system prompt instructions and instead read the response by block type.

steps.title: Re-evaluates and records again
steps.body: Evaluate the input bundle again after adjustment. If the criteria are satisfied, finalize and record the updated instructions in the model-specific override item of the standard template. If the criteria are not satisfied, return to the difference classification stage.

screens.outro: Now, let's examine the characteristic of the prompt where food costs increase.

screens.title: Explanation: Prompts that increase food costs
screens.lead: The following is a long, stacked hypothetical prompt tailored to match the habits of a single model. By selecting the indicated section, you can see why issues arise when the model changes.

data.text: You are a customer inquiry classifier. Print only the label. Never attach any description. Never use Markdown. If uncertain, just write "other". Think through the process, but do not output it—just provide the answer on the first line. The output must be exactly one word.

marks.span: Print only the label. Never attach any description.
marks.note: This is an indirect instruction accumulated to overcome the previous model's habit of adding explanations. The new model may not interpret it with the same intensity, and when the instruction is strong and the interpretation diverges, it becomes harder to locate. Output formatting is easier to transfer when clearly specified in one place.

Additional prohibitive instructions based on a specific model's expression habits. These may no longer be necessary or could lead to different habits when the model changes. As such instructions accumulate, the number of items to verify during model replacement increases.

Since this is a classification rule, it must maintain its meaning even after being extracted. However, in cases such as Model C where ambiguous queries are not sent to "other," verify that the rule is being followed by including ambiguous queries in the evaluation batch.

marks.span: Think through the process, but do not output it—just provide the answer on the first line.
marks.note: Instructions based on the inference mechanism of the model. For models where adaptive thinking operates by default even without a thinking field, such as Sonnet 5.5, the request settings or response handling must be re-evaluated.

marks.span: The output must be exactly one word.
marks.note: This sentence specifies the output format dependent on post-processing code. Instructions that concisely and clearly state such formats become the first criterion checked during integration.

screens.outro: I will summarize the factors increasing and decreasing costs on one page.

screens.title: Limits of Prompt Transferability and Responses
screens.lead: We divide and summarize the content of this course into limits, adjustment factors, and response measures.

paragraphs: **Limitations**: Even for the same sentence, different models exhibit variations in format, length, and instruction guidelines due to differences in how they interpret instructions, their default verbosity, and their default reasoning behaviors. Therefore, prompts are model-dependent and are not reusable assets that can simply be copied and pasted.

**Reconfiguration Elements**: When performing the migration, there are four components that need to be reconciled again. These are output format instructions, examples, request parameters, and response handling codes. The first two are located within the prompt, while the last two are outside the prompt.

**Response mechanisms**: Measure differences using evaluation input bundles, maintain a fixed skeleton via a standard template, and record instruction changes resulting from model-specific overrides. By keeping prompts short and explicit and incorporating evaluation bundles, migration costs are reduced. The magnitude of migration costs is determined by the number of instruction differences across models, the size of the evaluation bundle, and the format dependency of post-processing code.

When migrating to a new model, first read the change log of the migration guide for that model. Before making any prompt adjustments, verify that the request functions correctly. OpenAI's production documentation explains that model and generated token limits significantly affect performance, so when migrating, also check the output length specifications.

callout.label: Core
callout.text: Transplanting is not copying but a realignment after evaluation.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded or graded.
checks.q: When moving the customer inquiry classification prompt from Model A to Model B without changing a single character, Model B appended a reason sentence to the label, breaking the post-processing. What is the most appropriate explanation for this cause?
options: Some sentences were lost during the process of prompt copying.
Different models have varying instruction interpretation methods and baseline behaviors, causing the same sentence to be interpreted differently.
Post-processing code is model-agnostic, so there should be no difference in the format of model responses.
The B model has a structural limitation that prevents it from generating labels as a single word.
checks.explain: Even with the same prompt, differences in how instructions are interpreted, baseline verbosity, default reasoning settings, and other model characteristics cause variations in format and length. Therefore, model switching is not merely a change of a single configuration setting.

wrong.0: The sentence remained unchanged, so this is not a copy loss but a difference in model characteristics.
wrong.2: Post-processing code depends on the response format, so format differences directly become obstacles.
wrong.3: Enhancing the output instruction makes the difference identifiable, and there is no evidence to support this as a structural limitation.

checks.correctFeedback: Yes. The cause is not the prompt but the model's characteristics.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think again. The sentence is exactly the same, but the result has changed—this is the clue.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded or graded.
checks.q: What is the most appropriate way to handle standard prompt templates when there are differences in instructions by model?
options: Each model uses a completely new prompt from the beginning and does not compare them against each other.
Keep only the prompt from the highest-performing model and use it exactly across other models.
Evaluation input bundles are kept separate from templates and are created anew after the model is changed.
Roles, tasks, output formats, and example slots are kept fixed in structure, with model-specific instruction differences specified in override items.
checks.explain: When model-overwrite is applied on a fixed skeleton, the modified instruction is recorded, and when evaluation input bundles are stored together, they can be directly compared using the same bundle during model replacement.

wrong.0: Replacing everything entirely makes it impossible to track what has changed, and instead increases migration costs.
wrong.1: If you fix one model's format and instructions, you may overlook differences in format and instruction compliance across other models.
wrong.2: You must store evaluation groups together with templates so that when the model is changed, you can immediately compare the same inputs.

checks.correctFeedback: Yes. This is the approach of separating the fixed skeleton and override.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think about it again. We need a structure that can record only the changed parts.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded or graded.
checks.q: When replacing a model, consider the procedure of adjusting the prompt in the correct order.
items: Currently fixes the prompt, representative input bundle, and expected output based on the baseline.
In the new model, the same input is processed and differences are classified into three types: format, compliance instruction, and accuracy.
The format difference is adjusted by output instruction enhancement, and the accuracy difference is adjusted by adding examples.
Matches the request parameters and response handling codes against the guide's change log
Re-evaluate; if criteria are satisfied, finalize and record the overwrite of the updated instruction.
checks.explain: Baseline fixation, difference classification, adjustment, code reconciliation, reevaluation, and recording, in that order. A baseline must exist in order to objectively classify differences.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. It starts from the baseline and ends with reevaluation.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Let's take a closer look at the sequence. The reference line to be compared must come first.

glossary.def: This prompt can be used with other models at the same quality level.
This is a phenomenon where the same instruction sentence is interpreted or supported differently by different models, or due to different parameters.
This is a cycle where the difference between the baseline and the evaluation input is measured, the prompt is modified, and the evaluation is repeated.
A common skeleton and model-specific override items fixed for role, task, output format, and example slot.

misconceptions.myth: The same prompt yields the same result.
misconceptions.fact: Format, length, and instruction syntax vary depending on the model due to differences in instruction interpretation methods, baseline verbosity, and reasoning defaults.

misconceptions.myth: Translating just the prompt sentence completes the translation.
misconceptions.fact: Request parameters and response handling also change. For example, assistant prefill may return a 400 error in some models and may start its response with a safety block.

misconceptions.myth: Reading a few results visually is sufficient.
misconceptions.fact: To avoid missing differences, the same input batch must be compared against the baseline. A evaluation set is necessary to distinguish differences in format, compliance, and accuracy.

closing.lead: This summarizes the core content of the class.
points: Prompts are dependent on the model.
Transplanting is not copying but a realignment after evaluation.
Standard templates and evaluation bundles reduce migration costs.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Among our prompts, what will be most misaligned if we change the model, and how high will that cost be?
